tip: Verbs ending in -ier (étudier) have a double 'i' in the nous/vous forms: nous étudions, vous étudiez.
Apprendre (to learn) conjugates like prendre: j'apprends, tu apprends, il apprend, nous apprenons, ils apprennent.
Conduire (to drive) is irregular: je conduis, tu conduis, il conduit, nous conduisons, vous conduisez, ils conduisent.
'Avoir froid' = to be cold (feeling), 'avoir chaud' = to be hot. French says 'I have cold/heat' not 'I am cold/hot'.
'Avoir besoin de' = to need. Literally 'to have need of': j'ai besoin d'eau (I need water).
Payer can be spelled je paye or je paie – both are correct. Verbs ending in -ayer allow both forms.
'Partager' = to share/split. Keeps 'e' before -ons: 'nous partageons'. 'L'addition' = the bill.
Modals (vouloir, pouvoir, devoir) take the infinitive directly. je veux manger (I want to eat), il peut aider (he can help). No preposition between them.
Don't say je veux à manger – the à is wrong. Modal verb + bare infinitive, no preposition.
Ouvrir (to open) is irregular: j'ouvre, tu ouvres, il ouvre, nous ouvrons. Despite being -ir, it uses -er endings in present.
'Regarder' means 'to watch/look at' – the 'at' is built in. No preposition needed: je regarde la télé, not *je regarde à la télé.
'Jouer au' is used for sports (au football), while 'jouer du/de la' is for instruments (du piano). The preposition changes the meaning.
In French, meals take the definite article: 'le dîner' (dinner), 'le déjeuner' (lunch). English drops it; French doesn't.
'Adorer' = to love/adore. Stronger than 'aimer'. With general nouns, use the article: 'adorent le chocolat'.

target: Il passe ses vacances à Nice.
english: He spends his holidays in Nice.
tip: 'Passer' = to spend (time). With places, use `à` for cities: 'à Paris', 'à Nice'.
Aimer is a regular -er verb. Use aimer + definite article for general likes: J'aime le café (I like coffee in general).
'Porter' means both 'to carry' and 'to wear': context determines. 'Portent des lunettes' = they wear glasses.
'Finir de + infinitive' means 'to finish doing something'. This is a common -ir verb construction.
Arriver is a regular -er verb, but in passé composé it uses être as auxiliary: je suis arrivé(e). At A1, focus on present tense.
'Être en retard' = to be late. French uses the preposition 'en' before 'retard', not 'à' or nothing.
Partitive articles `du/de la/des` = 'some' (unspecified quantity). `Je mange du pain` = 'I eat some bread'. English often drops 'some'; French keeps the article.
Boire (to drink) is irregular: je bois, tu bois, il boit, nous buvons, vous buvez, ils boivent. Note the 'uv' in plural.
After negation, all partitives collapse to `de`: `je mange du pain` → `je ne mange pas de pain`. Watch out – easy to miss when speaking quickly.
Comprendre (to understand) conjugates like prendre: je comprends, tu comprends, il comprend, nous comprenons, ils comprennent.
For -er verbs ending in -ger (manger), add an extra 'e' before -ons: nous mangeons. This keeps the soft 'g' sound.
'Habiter à' is used with cities: 'habiter à Paris'. For countries, use 'habiter en' (feminine) or 'habiter au' (masculine).
Adverbs like 'très' (very) and 'bien' (well) go right after the verb in French: 'il danse très bien', not *il très bien danse.
The 'nous' form of -er verbs always ends in '-ons': chantons, parlons, jouons. It's the most regular pattern in French.
Verbs like acheter change è before silent endings: j'achète, tu achètes, il achète, but nous achetons (no accent change).
'Inviter' is regular -er. 'Des amis' uses partitive 'des' = some. French requires this where English omits 'some'.
'-ir' verbs like 'finir' add '-iss-' in plural forms. Think of it as the verb 'growing' when more people are involved.
'Choisir de' + infinitive = to choose to: 'Je choisis de rester' (I choose to stay). The 'de' is required.
With '-re' verbs, the il/elle form has no ending: 'il vend' (he sells). The 'd' is the last sound you hear.
'Entendre' = to hear (passive). 'Écouter' = to listen (active). Like English hear vs. listen.
'On' is an informal way to say 'we' in spoken French. It conjugates like il/elle (3rd person singular): on mange, on parle.
'Profiter de' means 'to enjoy/take advantage of'. The 'de' is required: profiter de la vie.
Lever changes the 'e' to 'è' before silent endings: je lève, tu lèves, il lève, but nous levons (no change).
French nouns are masculine or feminine, even objects. le pain (m, the bread), la pomme (f, the apple). Learn every noun with its article.
Envoyer changes its stem in some forms: j'envoie, tu envoies, il envoie, but nous envoyons. The 'y' becomes 'i' before silent endings.
'Garer' = to park. 'Garer la voiture' = to park the car. Reflexive 'se garer' = to park/find parking.
Verbs ending in -oyer (nettoyer) change 'y' to 'i' before silent endings: je nettoie, but nous nettoyons.
'Toucher' = to touch. Regular -er verb. 'Le mur' = the wall.
Ending hints: -e often f (la voiture), consonant or -eau often m (le pain, le bateau). Traps: le problème (m), la radio (f). The article is the real signal.
Interrompre conjugates like rompre: je romps, tu romps, il rompt (with a 't'), nous rompons.
With numbers, no article before the noun: 'deux enfants', not *'deux des enfants'. The number replaces the article.
`vous` is both 'you (plural)' and 'you (formal singular)'. Context decides. With strangers, in business, or with older people → vous. With friends, family, kids → tu.
Vouloir (to want) is irregular: je veux, tu veux, il veut, nous voulons, vous voulez, ils veulent. 'Je voudrais' is more polite.
Prendre (to take) is irregular: je prends, tu prends, il prend, nous prenons, vous prenez, ils prennent. Note double 'n' in plural.
Connaître (to know/be familiar with) is irregular: je connais, tu connais, il connaît, nous connaissons. Use for people/places/things.
Lire (to read) is irregular: je lis, tu lis, il lit, nous lisons, vous lisez, ils lisent.
'Être d'accord' = to agree. French uses 'to be of agreement' rather than a single verb.
Partir (to leave/depart) is irregular: je pars, tu pars, il part, nous partons, vous partez, ils partent.
Tenir (to hold) conjugates like venir: je tiens, tu tiens, il tient, nous tenons, vous tenez, ils tiennent.
Vivre (to live) is irregular: je vis, tu vis, il vit, nous vivons, vous vivez, ils vivent. Use for 'to live/be alive'.
'Nous' form of -er verbs: drop -er, add -ons. 'Préparons le petit déjeuner' = we prepare breakfast.
'Écouter' means 'to listen to' – the 'to' is built in. No preposition needed: j'écoute la musique (I listen to music).
'Téléphoner à' requires the preposition 'à' before the person: il téléphone à sa mère. Unlike 'appeler' which takes a direct object.
The 'tu' form of -er verbs always ends in '-es': tu nages, tu parles, tu manges. The final -s is always silent.
'Obéir à' = to obey. Regular -ir verb with -iss- in plural. Requires 'à': 'il obéit à ses parents'.
'Entrer dans' = to enter. Requires 'dans': 'vous entrez dans le magasin'. Uses 'être' in passé composé.
